answer_text:
Let a rotation in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) mean an element \(R \in SO(n)\), i.e. \(R^T R = I\) and \(\det R = 1\).

Suppose we are given \(k\) pairs
\[
(x_i, y_i), \qquad y_i = R(x_i),
\]
and assume the \(x_i\) are in general position, so that
\[
U = \operatorname{span}\{x_1,\dots,x_k\}
\]
has dimension \(k\). Then \(W=\operatorname{span}\{y_1,\dots,y_k\}\) also has dimension \(k\).

If one rotation \(R_0\) satisfies all \(k\) pairs, then any rotation \(A \in SO(n)\) that fixes every \(y_i\) also gives a valid rotation:
\[
(A R_0)(x_i)=A(R_0 x_i)=A y_i = y_i.
\]
So the ambiguity is exactly the subgroup of \(SO(n)\) that fixes \(W\) pointwise. That subgroup is isomorphic to
\[
SO(n-k).
\]

Thus \(k\) pairs determine \(R\) uniquely precisely when \(SO(n-k)\) is trivial. But
\[
SO(m)
\]
is trivial only for \(m=0\) or \(m=1\). Therefore we need
\[
n-k \le 1,
\]
so
\[
k \ge n-1.
\]

Conversely, \(n-1\) linearly independent pairs are enough: they determine the image of a hyperplane. The image of the unit normal to that hyperplane is then forced by the condition \(\det R=1\), choosing the normal direction with the correct orientation. Hence the action of \(R\) on a full basis is determined, so \(R\) itself is determined.

Therefore the minimum number of useful, independent pairs is

\[
\boxed{n-1}
\]

(with the trivial case \(n=1\) giving \(0\) pairs, since \(SO(1)=\{I\}\)).
